Add this shape to the scene, under the active layer of the scene it is bound to.
Clears the sticky `tmp()` flag — `addToScene()` is the documented way back in.

`scene` may be given explicitly (the usual case for a host that owns a root and is
adding a freshly built, never-attached shape); otherwise the shape's own node/carried
root is used. Returns `this` even when no scene is reachable, so it stays chainable.

entries.name: align
entries.sig: (other: AlignTarget, pivot?: string | PointLike, alignment?: string | PointLike): this
entries.doc:
Translate this shape so that the `pivot` point on its own bbox coincides with
the `alignment` point on `other`'s bbox.

Both `pivot` and `alignment` accept:
- A keyword string combining any of: left, right, front, back, top, bottom
  (unspecified axes default to the centre of that axis)
- A PointLike [x%, y%, z%] where 0 = min-side and 1 = max-side

`other` may be a Shape, a Point, or a raw PointLike; a point is treated as a
zero-size bbox at that location (as if it were a Vertex).
examples:
box.align(shelf, 'bottom', 'top')  // sits box on top of shelf
box.align(other, 'center', 'center') // centres box on other
box.align(curve.middle(), 'lefttop') // align to a bare point

entries.name: alignByPoints
entries.sig: (sourcePoints: [PointLike, PointLike, PointLike], targetPoints: [PointLike, PointLike, PointLike], withScale?: boolean): this
entries.doc:
Align this Curve by mapping 3 source points onto 3 target points.

- **withScale:** if true, apply a uniform scale (centered at q1) so edge lengths match.

params.name: sourcePoints
params.doc: 3 reference points on the curve (current space)

params.name: targetPoints
params.doc: 3 corresponding destination points

params.name: withScale
params.doc: optionally scale uniformly to match first-edge length

entries.name: alignTo
entries.sig: (other: AlignTarget, pivot?: string | PointLike, alignment?: string | PointLike): this
entries.doc: Alias for align()

entries.name: alpha
entries.doc: Alias for `opacity()`.

entries.name: annotations
entries.doc: Annotations linked to this Shape

entries.name: area
entries.doc:
Net area enclosed by this curve: the boundary area minus any interior holes
(e.g. from a boolean difference where the subtrahend lands fully inside).
Only valid for closed planar curves; warns and returns undefined otherwise.

entries.name: array
entries.doc: Arrange copies of this Curve in a 3-D array.
entries.returnsDoc: ShapeCollection<Curve> containing all copies (the original sits at [0,0,0]).

params.name: sizes
params.doc:
Number of copies along [x, y, z] axes (default [2, 2, 1]).
Non-integer values are floored; values < 1 map to 1.

params.name: offsets
params.doc:
Distance between copy origins along [x, y, z].
Defaults to the bbox extent on each axis so copies are placed adjacent.

entries.name: autoDim
entries.sig: (options?: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }, strategy?: string): any
entries.doc:
Automatic dimensioning of this shape (Annotator). `dim()` routes here by itself
for shapes a single bbox dimension cannot describe.

params.name: options
params.type: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }

entries.name: autoRotate
entries.doc:
Rotate this Curve to align as much as possible to the world axes.
Alias for rotateToOrtho()

entries.name: bbox
entries.doc:
Get Bbox from Curve. 
NOTE: If Curve is in 3D space, returns a 3D Bbox - if Curve is planar or not

entries.name: carbon
entries.doc: Embodied carbon (kgCO2e) of this shape. Defaults to cradle-to-gate A1-A3.

entries.name: center
entries.doc: Center point of this curve's bounding box

entries.name: chamfer
entries.doc:
Chamfer (bevel) the sharp corners of a Curve, cutting back `setback` along
each edge. Works on both closed and open curves (interior corners only).

params.name: at
params.doc: Optional corner filter — see fillet(). Omit to chamfer every corner.

entries.name: close
entries.doc:
Close this curve by adding a segment from end back to start.
If already closed, returns self unchanged.

entries.name: closestPoints
entries.doc:
Find the closest pair of points between this curve and another.
Uses coarse sampling + multi-seed alternating closest-point refinement.
Returns [pointOnThis, pointOnOther], or null if it cannot be determined.

entries.name: color
entries.sig: (color: string | number, g?: number, b?: number): this
entries.doc: Set color (both stroke and fill) of (closed) Curve

entries.name: colorGradient
entries.doc:
Colour this Curve with a gradient along its length.

```js
curve.colorGradient('red', 'blue')                        // two colours, end to end
curve.colorGradient('red', 'white', 'blue')               // evenly spaced
curve.colorGradient([[0,'red'], [0.5,'orange'], [1,'blue']])
curve.colorGradient([0,'red'], [0.5,'orange'], [1,'blue']) // the same, as varargs
```

Positions run 0 to 1 along the curve's ARC LENGTH, so a stop at 0.5 is halfway along the
drawn line whatever the tessellation does.

A stop is `[position, colour]` — a two-element array whose second element is not a
number. That matters because `[255,0,0]` is a colour, so `colorGradient([255,0,0],
[0,0,255])` is two colours while `colorGradient([0,'red'], [1,'blue'])` is two stops.

Rendered as per-vertex colour, so it stays ONE curve with one material rather than being
chopped into segments. Calling color afterwards clears the gradient.

entries.name: compoundMixedDegrees
entries.doc:
Native curves are uniformly (arc-length) parameterised, so there are no
mixed per-span degrees to guard against.

entries.name: connect
entries.doc:
Connect endpoints to endpoints of another Curve by creating Line
    and if possible create a single continuous (closed) curve

Setting the distance controls behaviour:
- maxGap = undefined: connect both endpoints unrelated to distance
- maxGap < distance(other) - can't connect
- maxGap >= distance(other) - connect closest endpoints

entries.name: containsPoint
entries.doc:
Whether a point lies inside this closed Curve — inside its outline and outside any of
its holes. False for an open or non-planar Curve (a point cannot be 'inside' those),
and for a point off the Curve's plane.

Decided by a crossing count against the curve's tessellation in its own plane, so a
point sitting ON the boundary (within the chord tolerance) is not answered reliably.
It is meant for points that are clearly in or out, such as the segment midpoints of an
intersection.

entries.name: continuous
entries.doc:
Draw this Curve as an unbroken line — the counterpart of dashed.

An empty dash pattern is what "no dashes" means throughout the pipeline (SVG omits
`stroke-dasharray`, glTF gets the all-ones 0xFFFF pattern), and setting it here marks
it EXPLICIT, so it wins in the style cascade: a curve on a `layer('diagram').dashed()`
can opt back out without the layer having to change. The name follows the DXF/CAD
linetype it exports as — CONTINUOUS.

entries.name: controlPoints
entries.doc: Get control points (native segment vertices) of the Curve

entries.name: copy
entries.doc:
Public copy. Clones via `_copy()`, then — unless this shape is `tmp()` — adds the
clone to the active layer. `copy()` means "give me a new shape", and new shapes render:
the clone is attached whenever a layer is reachable, which includes copying a DETACHED
but scene-derived shape (`curve.segments().first().copy()`) via the carried `_scene`.
The clone inherits the opaque `_modeler` and is flagged `_nameInherited` so the host
auto-namer can rename it after its variable.

Inside kernel operations use `_copy()` instead — it is the pure clone and never touches
the scene. Do NOT reach for `tmp()` there: `_suppressScene` is sticky and propagates to
every derived shape, so a tmp'd internal copy would suppress the real result too.

entries.name: cutoff
entries.sig: (at: Axis, coord?: number, smallest?: boolean): Curve | ShapeCollection<Curve>
entries.doc:
Cut off this Curve with the axis-aligned plane `{ <at> = coord }` and keep one piece —
the Curve twin of Mesh.cutoff() and Polygon.cutoff(). Keeps the biggest piece by default
(by length for an open Curve, by area for a closed one); `smallest=true` keeps the
smallest.

The plane meets the Curve's own plane in a line, and the Curve is cut by that line the
way cutoffBy() cuts it, with the same result: this Curve updated in place, or a
ShapeCollection when the kept part of an open Curve is several pieces. Returns the Curve
unchanged (with a warning) when the plane does not split it.

params.name: at
params.doc: World axis of the cutting plane's normal ('x' | 'y' | 'z').

params.name: coord
params.doc: Position of the plane along `at` (default 0).

params.name: smallest
params.doc: Keep the smallest piece instead of the biggest.

entries.name: cutoffBy
entries.doc:
Cut this Curve by another and keep the BIGGEST part of it — the same contract brep's
Shape.cutoffBy() has (split, then keep the largest piece). Set keepSmallest=true for the
smallest instead. Whatever kind of pair it is, the result is a part of THIS Curve.

- Open this Curve (e.g. a line): split at the intersection point(s) with other
  and keep the biggest/smallest segment.
- Closed this Curve + open other (e.g. a line crossing it): split the closed
  curve along the cutter into two regions and keep the biggest/smallest by area.
- Closed this Curve + closed other: split into the part inside the cutter and the part
  outside it, and keep the biggest/smallest by area.

entries.name: difference
entries.doc:
Boolean subtraction: this Curve minus one or more cutters.

Cutters can be single Curves, ShapeCollections of Curves, or any mix of the two, so
`band.difference(layer('rafters').shapes())` works like it does on Mesh and Polygon.
All curves must be closed and coplanar. Two kinds of cutter are skipped with a warning
rather than wrecking the result: members of a collection that are not Curves, and a
cutter that IS this very Curve — a layer collection routinely contains the very shape
you are cutting, and subtracting a region from itself leaves nothing.

Cutters are applied in order, each one to every piece produced so far, so a cutter that
splits the region in two is still followed correctly by the next cutter. A cutter whose
boolean fails is skipped (warning) and its piece kept, so one bad cutter in a collection
no longer costs you the whole result.

Returns the exterior outlines of the resulting regions: this Curve when a single region
is left (geometry replaced in place), a ShapeCollection<Curve> when the cut split it into
several (this Curve unchanged), or null when the cutters removed everything — or, for a
single cutter, when the boolean failed outright.

entries.name: dim
entries.sig: (options?: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }): any
entries.doc: Alias for dimension().

params.name: options
params.type: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }

entries.name: dimension
entries.sig: (options?: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }): any
entries.doc: Create dimension line(s) for this shape (Annotator).

params.name: options
params.type: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }

entries.name: direction
entries.doc: Direction vector from start to end point (not normalised)

entries.name: dispose
entries.doc:
Release the underlying kernel curve (and any holes) immediately.

wasm-bindgen registers a `FinalizationRegistry` for every kernel object, so this is not
required for correctness — but GC finalisation is non-deterministic and applies no
back-pressure on WASM linear memory. A host that keeps curves alive across a long
session (a CAD document rather than a one-shot script) should free them explicitly on
delete. Mirrors `Mesh.dispose()`.

After `dispose()` the curve is unusable: `inner()` will throw.

entries.name: distance
entries.doc:
Minimum distance to another PointLike or Curve
Returns null if the closest parameter cannot be determined.

entries.name: edges
entries.doc: For BREP compatibility: alias for segments()

entries.name: end
entries.doc: End point of the curve (arc-length parameter 1).

entries.name: exportSpans
entries.doc:
spanParams, with consecutive conic spans of the same ellipse merged.

hypercurve splits an ellipse into spans of at most 90° so every conic weight stays
positive, so a full ellipse arrives as four spans of one shape. A format that has
an ellipse primitive (DXF `ELLIPSE`, SVG `A`) wants that back as one entity, and
both writers want it identically — hence one implementation here rather than two
that drift.

Spans that are not conics, and conics whose ellipse could not be reconstructed,
pass through untouched.

entries.name: extend
entries.doc:
Extend the curve by `length` at its start / end / both, along the endpoint
tangent(s). Rebuilds as a polyline through the extended vertices.

entries.name: extendTo
entries.doc:
Extend this curve to another curve or shape collection.
Fires a probe ray from each end along its tangent direction, finds where it meets
`other`, and extends the nearer end by that amount.

A REAL crossing always wins over a closest-approach guess, whichever end it is on:
the whole ray is searched for true intersections first, and only when nothing crosses
does it fall back to the nearest approach (which is what makes `extendTo()` work for
converging-but-not-meeting curves). Without that order a curve that genuinely crosses
a target 300 away could lose to the *other* end drifting within 4 of it, and the wrong
end would move.

entries.name: extrude
entries.doc:
Extrude this curve along a direction to create a Mesh.
If the curve is closed and planar, creates a solid extrusion.
If the curve is open or non-planar, creates a swept surface.
entries.returnsDoc:
A new Mesh representing the extruded geometry

NOTE: bring this into the Rust/WASM layer?

params.name: length
params.doc: The extrusion length (default: 1)

params.name: direction
params.doc: The extrusion direction vector (default planar normal or [0,0,1])

entries.name: fillet
entries.doc:
Fillet (round) the sharp corners of a Curve with arcs of `radius`.
Works on both closed curves (every corner) and open curves (interior corners
only — the two free endpoints are not corners). Corners where the radius does
not fit are left sharp.

params.name: at
params.doc:
Optional corner filter: only these corners are filleted. Accepts a
corner index (negative counts from the end), a point (the nearest
corner wins), a Vertex, a selector string, a ShapeCollection, or an
array mixing those. Omit to fillet every corner.

NOTE: a flat array of numbers is always read as a point — `[0, 2]` is
the point (0,2), not corners 0 and 2, because the two are
indistinguishable. Pass several indices as a Uint32Array.

examples: curve.fillet(5, [10, 10, 0])             // the corner nearest that point
curve.fillet(5, 'vertex<<->[0,0,0]')     // the corner nearest the origin

entries.name: filletAtParams
entries.doc: Fillet only the corners nearest the given curve parameters.

entries.name: first
entries.doc:
The first shape of a single Shape is the Shape itself.

Ops that MAY split — `cutoffBy()`, `difference()`, `intersections()` — answer with one
Shape or with a ShapeCollection depending on the geometry, and a script cannot know which
in advance. `first()` lets the same line read either: `post.cutoffBy(diagonal).first()`.
brep's Shape carries the same method for the same reason.

entries.name: flatten
entries.doc:
Flatten this Curve onto a coordinate plane: project it onto the plane through the
origin perpendicular to `axis` and drop the doubles that creates — segments that
collapse onto each other (the two vertical edges of a wall outline) or onto nothing
(an edge running along the axis). Mirrors Mesh.flatten() / ShapeCollection.flatten().

params.name: axis
params.doc: Axis to collapse along ('x' | 'y' | 'z', default 'z' — onto the XY plane).

entries.name: getOnPlane
entries.sig: (tolerance?: number): { normal: Vector; x: Vector; y: Vector }
entries.doc:
Get the plane of the Curve as { normal, x, y }.
The local axes are aligned to the closest global axes.
Returns null if the curve is not planar.

entries.name: grid
entries.sig: (cx?: number, cy?: number, cz?: number, spacing?: PointLike): ShapeCollection<Curve>
entries.doc:
Arrange copies of this Curve on a 3-D grid.
Counts are floored and clamped to at least 1, so `grid(4, 3, 0)` is a flat 4x3 grid
in XY rather than an empty collection.
entries.returnsDoc:
ShapeCollection<Curve> of all copies - this Curve itself is the copy at
cell [0,0,0] (like row()), so the scene never gets a duplicate on top of it.

params.name: spacing
params.doc: Distance between copy origins, uniform or per axis.

entries.name: hasArcs
entries.doc:
Whether this curve is curved anywhere — a circular arc, or any conic, Bézier or
spline span. False for pure line work.

entries.name: hasHoles
entries.doc: Check if this curve has interior holes

entries.name: holes
entries.doc: Get interior hole curves (if any, e.g. from boolean difference creating a hole)

entries.name: intersect
entries.doc:
Replace this Curve by its intersection with another Curve or Mesh, the way union() and
difference() replace it by their result — the mesh-kernel spelling of brep's intersect().

A single Curve piece updates this Curve in place; anything else (the Vertices where two
open curves cross, or several pieces) is a new shape that takes this Curve's place in the
scene. Nothing shared leaves this Curve alone and returns null. Use intersections() /
intersection() to keep this Curve and get the result as a new shape.

entries.name: intersection
entries.doc:
The single shared shape between this Curve and another Curve or Mesh — the singular of
intersections(), with the same non-replacing, added-to-the-active-layer contract.

`line.intersection(rect)` is the piece of line inside the rect, and its `vertices()` are
the two crossings — which is how you ask for intersection POINTS. Two open curves have
nothing but crossings, so they answer with those Vertices directly.

entries.name: intersections
entries.doc:
The geometry this Curve shares with another Curve or a Mesh: the Curve piece(s) where
they overlap along a length, the Vertices where they only cross. See _intersectionCurve()
for what each kind of pair answers.

NON-REPLACING: this Curve is left exactly as it is; the results are NEW shapes that are
added to the active layer, so they are visible without an explicit addToScene(). Mark
this Curve tmp() to keep the results out of the scene. Use intersect() to replace this
Curve by the intersection instead.

entries.name: is2D
entries.doc: Whether this curve lies in a 2D plane (zero extent on one axis)

entries.name: is3D
entries.doc:
Whether this Shape has extent along all three axes — the complement of is2D(), which
Mesh and Curve each define from their bbox. Kept on the base class because callers
outside meshup (the host annotator deciding which way to offset a dimension line) ask
any Shape, and a missing method there is a crash, not a `false`.

entries.name: isCompound
entries.doc: A curve is "compound" when it has more than one native segment.

entries.name: isCuboid
entries.doc:
Whether this Curve is essentially a cuboid (rectangle in 2D).

A single line is 1D and never a cuboid. For 2D-or-bigger curves, builds
the OBB and checks every tessellated point: each point must
sit on the OBB surface — within ±halfExtent on every non-zero axis and
touching at least one face — within `tolerance`. Arcs / circles /
splines / non-rect polylines fail; tessellated rectangles pass even
when sides are subdivided.

entries.name: isCurve
entries.doc: True for curve-like shapes: mesh Curve (brep Edge/Wire once wired).

entries.name: iso
entries.sig: (cam?: PointLike, method?: HlrStrategy, options?: ProjectionOptions): ShapeCollection<any>
alt: (cam?: PointLike, hiddenLines?: boolean, includeHiddenShapes?: boolean, samples?: number, featureAngle?: number, view?: ProjectionViewOptions): ShapeCollection<any>
entries.doc: Shorthand alias for isometry.

entries.name: isometry
entries.sig: (cam?: PointLike, method?: HlrStrategy, options?: ProjectionOptions): ShapeCollection<any>
alt: (cam?: PointLike, hiddenLines?: boolean, includeHiddenShapes?: boolean, samples?: number, featureAngle?: number, view?: ProjectionViewOptions): ShapeCollection<any>
entries.doc:
Isometric projection of this Curve.

A Curve is line work already, so there is nothing to remove hidden lines
*from* — but it is geometry in the drawing, and it projects onto the same
screen plane as everything else. Projecting one on its own gives the
flattened, screen-oriented result you would get from a collection
containing only it.

To have a solid hide part of this curve, put both in a
ShapeCollection and project that: the collection is what knows
about the occluders. See `ShapeCollection.isometry`.

params.name: cam
params.doc: Direction from the origin toward the viewer. Default `[-1,-1,1]`.

params.name: method
params.doc:
Which hidden-line algorithm the projection runs. Only
matters when there are solids to hide things; kept for signature
parity with Mesh.isometry.

params.name: options
params.doc: Projection settings — see ProjectionOptions.

entries.name: isShapeClass
entries.doc: Implement this and ShapeCollection allows it

entries.name: isSolid
entries.doc: True for solid-like shapes: mesh Mesh (brep Shell/Solid once wired).

entries.name: isStraight
entries.doc:
Whether this curve is straight (all defining vertices collinear).

Answered from native geometry, never from a tessellation: an arc-bearing curve is
straight by definition never, and for line-only geometry the defining vertices ARE
the curve, so testing them is exact as well as O(segments) instead of O(samples).

entries.name: knots
entries.doc:
The spline's knot vector.

A curve carried by a single NURBS span (e.g. from Curve.Interpolated)
returns its real knot vector. Line/arc geometry has no explicit knot vector — it is
re-parameterised by arc length — so that falls back to the parameter domain `[0, 1]`.

entries.name: label
entries.sig: (value: string, options?: { angle?: number; arrow?: boolean; circle?: boolean; class?: string; labelOnly?: boolean; length?: number; … }): any
entries.doc: Attach a free-text label at this shape's center (Annotator).

params.name: options
params.type: { angle?: number; arrow?: boolean; circle?: boolean; class?: string; labelOnly?: boolean; length?: number; … }

entries.name: layflat
entries.doc:
Rotate the curve to lay flat on the XY plane, then drop it so its lowest point sits at Z = 0.
Uses a shortest-arc rotation to align the thinnest OBB axis with world +Z, leaving the
in-plane orientation untouched (avoids instability for symmetric curves with equal eigenvalues).

entries.name: loft
entries.sig: (others: Curve | Curve[], solid?: boolean): Mesh | Polygon
entries.doc:
Loft a ruled surface/solid through this curve and one or more other curves.
Builds a ruled mesh by stitching the tessellated profiles.

- **Open profiles** → a lofted surface. Two straight open curves give a single flat
  `Polygon` (quad); any other open loft returns a triangulated surface `Mesh`.
- **Closed profiles** → a `Mesh`. With `solid = true` (default) end caps are added at
  the first and last profile for a watertight solid; with `solid = false` only the
  open tube wall is returned.
entries.returnsDoc: A new Mesh or Polygon, or null on invalid input.

params.name: others
params.doc: A single Curve or an array of Curves to loft through (in order after this).

params.name: solid
params.doc: When all profiles are closed, cap the ends into a watertight solid (default true).

entries.name: material
entries.doc: Assign (setter, chainable) or read (getter → BoundMaterial) this shape's material.

entries.name: maxDegree
entries.doc: Get maximum degree over the native segments.

entries.name: mergeColinearLines
entries.doc:
Merge runs of adjacent, same-direction line segments into single segments.

Collinearity is decided exactly by hypercurve, which compares the segments' supports
rather than measuring an angle against a tolerance. It also keeps what a tolerance test
gets wrong: arcs are preserved (this used to refuse any curve containing one), the
closed seam is considered like any other joint, and a collinear *reversal* is left
alone — a spike doubling back on itself is authored topology, not a redundant vertex.

`colinearTol` is accepted and ignored; there is no tolerance to spend.

entries.name: middle
entries.doc: Point at the midpoint of the curve by arc length

entries.name: mirror
entries.doc:
Mirror Curve across a plane defined by a direction (Axis or normal vector) and an optional position.
If no position is given, the bbox center of the curve is used.
Works by reflecting each NURBS control point across the plane: P' = P - 2·(dot(P−Q, n))·n

entries.name: move
entries.sig: (px: PointLike, dy?: number, dz?: number): this

entries.name: moveTo
entries.sig: (target: PointLike, py?: number, pz?: number): this
entries.doc:
Move this Curve so its bbox centre lands on `target`. Takes loose coordinates too
(`moveTo(200, 475, 0)`) - this override used to drop everything but the first
argument, silently moving the Curve to y=0/z=0 while Mesh.moveTo() did the right thing.

entries.name: name
alt: (): string
entries.doc:
Get or set a name for this shape (stored in metadata).
- Called with a string: sets the name and returns this (chainable).
- Called with no arguments: returns the current name or undefined.

entries.name: node
entries.doc: Return the SceneNode this curve belongs to, or null.

entries.name: nodeString
entries.doc:
Scene membership of this Shape, as shown by every toString(): the node holding it,
or that it is not in the scene at all.

entries.name: normal
entries.doc:
Get normal of planar Curve, returns null if not planar 
IMPORTANT: This method returns consistent normals independent of curve orientation
          Use normalOrientation() to get orientation-dependent normal if needed

entries.name: normalOrientation
entries.doc: Get normal based on curve orientation, returns null if not planar

entries.name: obbox
entries.doc:
Get the oriented bounding box of this Curve: the tightest (minimum-area) box around a
planar curve, the PCA box for a curve that runs through 3D.

entries.name: offset
entries.doc:
Offset a Curve a given amount (+grows / −shrinks).

`cornerType` decides how a convex corner is reconnected, and is honoured now — it used
to be accepted and dropped, so every corner behaved as `'smooth'`:
- `'sharp'` (default): the corner stays a point, mitred wherever a miter exists.
- `'round'`: an arc of radius `|distance|` centred on the original corner.
- `'smooth'`: mitred, but a corner sharper than ~29° — whose miter would run out past
  four times the offset distance — is arced instead. The historical behaviour.

entries.name: onClick
entries.doc: Make this shape clickable in the viewer and react to selection.

entries.name: opacity
entries.doc: Set opacity of (closed) Curve

entries.name: perpendicularPointTo
alt: (point: PointLike, all: true): Point[]
(point: PointLike, all?: boolean): Point | Point[]
entries.doc:
Find the point on this Curve where the line from the given point to that point
is perpendicular to the Curve (the foot of the perpendicular).

By default the *nearest* such point is returned. Some points have no perpendicular foot at
all — beyond the end of a line, or straight out from the corner of a rectangle — and then
the closest point on the Curve is returned instead.

Pass `all = true` to get every perpendicular foot instead (a circle seen from outside
has two, a wavy curve can have many), sorted by distance ascending. That list contains
only genuine perpendicular feet and may be empty.

NOTE: feet are computed on the curve's tessellation, so on arcs and ellipses they are
accurate to the kernel chord tolerance (~1e-4).

params.name: point
params.doc: the point to drop the perpendicular from

entries.name: pointAtPerc
entries.doc: Get point at given percentage of the curve length

entries.name: points
entries.doc: Alias for controlPoints

entries.name: projectOnto
entries.sig: (plane: BasePlane | { normal: PointLike; origin?: PointLike }): this
entries.doc: Project this Curve onto a plane, flattening all control points onto it.

params.name: plane
params.doc:
a named base plane ('xy', 'yz', 'xz', 'front', 'back', 'left', 'right')
or an object { normal: PointLike, origin?: PointLike } for an arbitrary plane.
If no origin is given for a custom plane, the world origin [0,0,0] is used.

entries.name: removeFromScene
entries.doc: Remove this shape from the scene (detaches its SceneNode). Returns `this`.

entries.name: replicate
entries.sig: (num: number, transform: (curve: Curve, index: number, prev: Curve) => Curve): ShapeCollection<Curve>
entries.doc: Replicate this Curve a given number of times and return in a ShapeCollection<Curve>

params.name: transform
params.type: (curve: Curve, index: number, prev: Curve) => Curve

entries.name: resetStyle
entries.doc:
Drop every style set on this Shape, back to the defaults.

A fresh Style rather than a cleared one, so the "explicitly set"
bookkeeping resets too: after this the Shape contributes nothing of its
own to the scene's style cascade, exactly as if it had never been styled.
That is the difference between this and setting the properties back to
their default values by hand, which would keep overriding a parent.

entries.name: reverse
entries.doc:
Reverse the direction of this curve (swap start/end).
Returns self for chaining.

entries.name: revolve
entries.sig: (angle?: number, axisStart?: PointLike | Axis, axisEnd?: PointLike | Axis, segments?: number): Mesh
entries.doc:
Revolve this curve around an axis into a Mesh — the lathe operation.

- **Closed profile** → a solid. A full turn closes on itself; a partial one is shut
  with a flat cap at either end, so the result is watertight either way.
- **Open profile** → a swept surface. It still comes out a closed solid when the
  profile begins and ends on the axis: a half circle revolves into a sphere.

Interior holes (left behind by a boolean difference) are revolved along with the
boundary, so a profile with a hole in it gives a solid with a matching cavity.

The axis can be given as two points (`axisStart` → `axisEnd`), as a single direction
through the world origin (`revolve(90, 'z')`), or left out altogether — then it is
detected from the curve: the world axis (Z first, then Y, then X) that lies in the
profile's own plane and that the profile does not straddle. A profile that straddles
its axis sweeps through itself; that is warned about, never silently corrected.
entries.returnsDoc: A new Mesh, or null on invalid input.

params.name: angle
params.doc: Sweep in degrees, negative to sweep the other way. Default 360, clamped to ±360.

params.name: axisStart
params.doc: Axis base point — or the axis direction, when `axisEnd` is left out.

params.name: axisEnd
params.doc: A second point on the axis.

params.name: segments
params.doc: Facets around the sweep (default: the quality profile's count for a full turn).

entries.name: rotate
entries.sig: (angle: number, axis?: PointLike | Axis, pivot?: PointLike): this
entries.doc:
Rotate the given curve a specified angle (in degrees) around an axis through the WORLD
ORIGIN — the explicitly origin-based turn, as on Mesh and Polygon. Pass a pivot, or use
rotateAround() / rotateX() / rotateY() / rotateZ(), to turn about the curve's own centre.

entries.name: rotateAround
entries.sig: (angleDeg: number, axis?: PointLike | Axis, pivot?: PointLike): this
entries.doc:
Rotate Curve by angleDeg around an axis through a pivot point.
Uses Rodrigues' rotation formula on control points — works for any axis.

params.name: angleDeg
params.doc: rotation angle in degrees

params.name: axis
params.doc: 'x' | 'y' | 'z' or an arbitrary direction vector (PointLike)

params.name: pivot
params.doc: point the axis passes through (default: this Curve's own center)

entries.name: rotateQuaternion
entries.sig: (wOrObj: number | { w: number; x: number; y: number; z: number }, x?: number, y?: number, z?: number): this
entries.doc:
Rotate Curve by a quaternion given as components `(w, x, y, z)`.
The quaternion is normalized internally, so non-unit input is safe.

params.name: wOrObj
params.type: number | { w: number; x: number; y: number; z: number }

entries.name: rotateToAxesOBbox
entries.doc:
Rotate this Curve so its oriented bounding box lines up with the world axes:
the OBB's thinnest axis onto +Z first, then its longest axis onto +X.
For a planar Curve the thinnest axis is the plane normal, so this lays it flat
on the XY plane (without moving it there — use layflat() for that).
Position of the center is kept.

entries.name: rotateToOrtho
entries.doc:
Rotate this Curve to align it with the world axes as much as possible.

First `rotateToAxesOBbox()` brings the curve flat onto the XY plane, then it is
turned around Z so its dominant segment direction lands on the X or Y axis.
The second step only ever turns around Z (by at most a quarter turn), so it can
never undo the flat alignment of the first.

params.name: o
params.doc:
'vertical' (default) puts the dominant segment direction on the Y axis,
'horizontal' puts it on the X axis

entries.name: rotateVecToVec
entries.sig: (from: PointLike, to: PointLike, pivot?: PointLike): this
entries.doc:
Rotate this Curve so that direction `from` ends up pointing along `to`, using the
shortest arc between the two.

params.name: pivot
params.doc: point the rotation turns around (default: this Curve's center)

entries.name: row
entries.sig: (count: number, spacing?: number, direction?: PointLike | Axis): ShapeCollection<Curve>
entries.doc:
Create a row of copies of this Curve with specific spacing between them

Spacing is measured from the bounding boxes of the curves, so they are placed adjacent plus the specified spacing.

params.name: count
params.doc: number of copies in the row (including the original)

params.name: spacing
params.doc: distance between bounding boxes of copies (default: 10)

params.name: direction
params.doc: direction of the row (default: 'x')

entries.name: scale
entries.doc: Scale Curve with a uniform factor or per-axis [sx, sy, sz] around an origin (default: center of this Curve)

entries.name: segment
entries.doc:
Copy a range of this Curve's atomic segments (see segments()) and combine them
into a single Curve.

Segments are taken in forward order from `fromIndex` to `toIndex` (both inclusive).
When `fromIndex > toIndex` the range wraps around the end of a *closed* curve
(its last segment joins back to its first), e.g. `segment(-1, 0)` on a closed rect
returns the last + first edge. Wrapping an open curve is an error.
entries.returnsDoc: a single Curve — one span stays a plain Curve, multiple spans become a CompoundCurve.

params.name: fromIndex
params.doc: first segment index (inclusive, 0-based). Negative indexes count from the end.

params.name: toIndex
params.doc: last segment index (inclusive). Defaults to fromIndex (single segment). Negative indexes count from the end.

entries.name: segmentCount
entries.doc: Number of exact spans.

entries.name: segments
entries.doc:
Return all atomic segments of this Curve.
- degree-1 spans (polylines) are split into individual line segments (N CPs → N-1 edges)
- higher-degree spans (arcs, splines) are returned as-is, one per span

entries.name: select
entries.doc:
Select (sub)shapes from this Curve using a selector string (see Selector.ts).
Supported shapes for a Curve target: `vertex` (control points),
`curve`/`wire` (the curve itself or its spans).
Selectors are greedy: an underspecified selector returns every match.
A ShapeCollection result is collapsed to the single shape when there is
exactly one match (checkSingle), and an empty result warns.
Selecting does not add anything to the scene - it hands back a reference to
geometry that is already there. `select(…).copy()` is what puts a new shape in.

entries.name: selected
entries.doc: True when this shape is currently selected (clicked) in the viewer.

entries.name: selfIntersecting
entries.doc:
Whether the curve crosses itself away from its own shared vertices.

hypercurve decides this with the predicates its intersection kernel uses, so a bulge
that grazes a leg is found from the arc rather than from however finely it happened to
be sampled. This used to project onto the curve's plane and run an O(n²) crossing test
over a tessellation in TypeScript.

entries.name: setId
entries.doc:
Overwrite this shape's id. Ids are minted per construction, so a shape rebuilt from
a saved document would otherwise come back with a fresh uuid and lose every reference
to it (scene links, host selection, undo entries). Deserialisers call this to restore
identity; nothing else should.

entries.name: sid
entries.doc: Serial id: the order this shape entered the scene, or 0 if it never did. See `_sid`.

entries.name: spanParams
entries.doc:
Every exact span, described by the parameters a file format needs to write it.

One entry per span, in order, matching segmentCount. Each is tagged by
`kind`, and arcs and conics carry the centre, radius, sweep and axes of the circle
or ellipse they lie on.

Use this, not the other accessors, when writing a file. They answer coarser
questions: subtype names the whole curve and has no name for "lines and
arcs mixed"; controlPoints returns span endpoints, which for an arc is its
chord; knots and weights are empty unless the whole curve is one
NURBS span. Writers built on those had to guess, and guessed wrong — an arc's
radius was re-derived from a circumcircle of tessellation samples, and a filleted
rectangle was written as a malformed DXF SPLINE built from its chords.

entries.name: split
entries.doc:
Split the curve at parameter t, returning [left, right]. 
Parameter t must be within the curve's knot domain.

entries.name: start
entries.doc: Start point of the curve (arc-length parameter 0).

entries.name: strokeWidth
entries.doc:
Line width in SCREEN PIXELS — not model units.

It travels to the viewer as `BENTLEY_materials_line_style.width` and becomes a pixel
`linewidth` on the fat-line material, so a line keeps the same apparent weight however
far you zoom. `thickness(4)` is four pixels, not four millimetres.

entries.name: subtype
entries.doc:
Classify this curve as 'Line'|'Arc'|'Circle'|'Rect'|'Polyline'|'Spline'|'Ellipse'.
Delegates to the native segment-based classification in Curve3DJs.

entries.name: tangent
entries.doc:
The tangent direction of a STRAIGHT Curve, as a normalised Vector.

A straight Curve has one tangent along its whole length, so it needs no point to be
asked at. Anything that curves has a different tangent at every point of it: there is
no single answer to give, so `tangent()` warns and returns null and `tangentAt(point)`
is the method to use. Falling back to the start→end chord would be worse than nothing —
on an arc that direction is the curve's tangent nowhere except by accident, and on a
closed curve it is the zero vector.

Straightness is read from the native geometry (`isStraight()`), so a Polyline whose
vertices happen to be collinear answers too — it has one tangent just as a Line does.

entries.name: tangentAt
entries.doc:
Get the tangent direction at the closest point on the curve to the given point.
Returns a normalised Vector, or null if the closest parameter cannot be found.

On a straight Curve the answer is the same everywhere — `tangent()` gives it without
needing a point.

entries.name: tessellate
entries.doc:
Tessellate the curve into a series of points.

How dense the result is comes from the quality profile — see `setQuality()` — which
sizes an arc by how far it *turns*, so a circle costs the same at any radius.
entries.returnsDoc: array of points representing the tessellated curve

params.name: tol
params.doc:
chord deviation as a **fraction of the span's own size**, overriding the
profile for this call. Not a distance in model units: `1e-4` means "within 0.01%
of the radius", which is the same request whether the model is in metres or in
millimetres. Roughly, `1e-2` → 22 facets per full turn, `1e-3` → 70, `1e-4` → 222.

entries.name: thickness
entries.doc: Alias for `strokeWidth()`. Reads more naturally for a curve. Screen pixels.

entries.name: tmp
entries.doc:
Mark this shape as temporary: detach it from the scene AND set a sticky
`_suppressScene` flag so that every subsequent scene op (copy/extrude/split/…) on it
is a no-op and every shape derived from it is `tmp()` too. Ideal for building helper
geometry inside advanced methods. `addToScene()` (host) clears the flag. Returns `this`.

entries.name: toBuffer
entries.doc:
Return raw tessellated points as a flat Float32Array (xyz per point, no axis remapping).
Used by GLTFBuilder to assemble GLTF geometry.

entries.name: toDegree1
entries.doc:
Create new Curve by tessellating any (compound) curve with degree > 1 into a degree-1 polyline,
then run `mergeColinearLines()` to collapse redundant collinear segments.
Curves that are already fully degree-1 are returned unchanged.

params.name: tol
params.doc: tessellation tolerance; defaults to the quality profile's.

entries.name: toFace
entries.doc: Alias for toPolygon()

entries.name: toGLB
entries.doc: Export this curve as a GLB binary (Uint8Array, LINE_STRIP).

entries.name: toGLTF
entries.doc: Export this curve as a self-contained GLTF JSON string (LINE_STRIP).

entries.name: toPathData
entries.doc:
This curve as SVG **path-data** — just the `d`, no element, no style attributes.

Differs from `toSVGElem()` in three ways that matter to a host renderer:
 - a `Circle` comes back as real path-data (two 180° arc spans), where `toSVGElem()`
   returns `<circle cx cy r/>` with no `d` at all;
 - interior holes are included as additional `M…Z` subpaths;
 - the Y convention is selectable. `flipY: true` (default) matches `toSVGElem()` and
   SVG's y-down screen space for a y-up curve. Pass `flipY: false` when the curve is
   ALREADY in y-down coordinates — that is also the form `Importer.fromSVG` reads back,
   so `Curve.fromData(c.toData())` round-trips without a mirror (which would tessellate
   arcs).

Lines and circular arcs are exact; splines are emitted as `Q`/`C` Béziers.

entries.name: toPolygon
entries.doc: Convert this curve to a Polygon via tessellation (including hole rings if present).

entries.name: toSVG
entries.doc:
Export this curve as a self-contained SVG string.
Assumes the curve is already 2D (on the XY plane).
Preserves arc geometry: degree-2 rational NURBS → SVG `A`, quadratic → `Q`, cubic → `C`, line → `L`.

entries.name: toSVGElem
entries.sig: (cssClass?: string, styleOpts?: { nonScalingStroke?: boolean; omitDefaults?: boolean }): string
entries.doc:
Return just the SVG element for this curve (`<path>` or `<circle>`),
without the outer `<svg>` wrapper. Used by SceneNode to compose hierarchies.
Assumes the curve is already 2D (on the XY plane). Use `is2D()` to check first.

`styleOpts` is passed straight to Style.toSvgAttrs — see there for why
non-scaling-stroke is opt-in and what omitDefaults is for.

entries.name: translate
entries.sig: (px: PointLike, dy?: number, dz?: number): this

entries.name: trim
alt: (at: Axis, coord?: number, smallest?: boolean): Curve | ShapeCollection<Curve>
(other: Curve, keepSmallest?: boolean): Curve | ShapeCollection<Curve>
entries.doc:
Keep the part of this Curve between two positions along its length, given as fractions
of the length in [0, 1] (`trim(0.25, 0.75)` keeps the middle half). Mutates in place
and returns `this`; the result is always an open Curve.

entries.name: union
entries.doc:
Boolean union of this (closed) Curve with another (closed) Curve.
Both curves must be closed and coplanar.
Returns the exterior outlines of the resulting regions,
or null on error.

entries.name: vertices
entries.doc:
Corner vertices along this Curve, in order.
- a straight line or single arc/spline span yields [start, end]
- polylines and rects yield every corner (segment junction) vertex
Coincident consecutive points (including the wrap for closed curves) are
collapsed, so a closed rect returns its 4 distinct corners.

entries.name: volume
entries.doc: Curves have no volume — returns undefined

entries.name: wasmPtr
entries.doc: Get inner WASM pointer — useful for debugging only. Use id() for stable identity.

entries.name: weight
entries.doc: Mass/weight in the active unit system. Shortcut for material().weight().

entries.name: weights
entries.doc:
The spline's per-control-point weights.

A curve carried by a single NURBS span returns its real weights. Native line/arc
geometry carries none (an arc is exact, not a weighted rational control net), so
that returns an empty array.

entries.name: Arc
entries.sig: (start: PointLike, mid: PointLike, end: PointLike, method?: "threepoint" | "tangent"): Curve
entries.doc:
Build an arc (a portion of a circle).

Two methods are available:

- `'threepoint': `start`, `mid`, `end` are three points on the arc.
   The three points must not be collinear.

- `'tangent'`: `start` is the start point, `mid` is the tangent direction at start,
   and `end` is the end point. The tangent must not be parallel to start→end.

entries.name: bboxOf
entries.doc:
Bbox of anything an alignment can target: a Shape, a ShapeCollection, or a bare point.
A Point / PointLike behaves like a Vertex: a zero-size bbox at that location.

entries.name: bboxPercToPoint
entries.doc: Resolve a [x%, y%, z%] percentage triple to a world-space Point within `bb`.

entries.name: bboxPointOf
entries.doc:
Resolve an alignment spec — a corner keyword ('lefttop') or a [x%, y%, z%] triple —
to a world-space Point on `bb`.

entries.name: Circle
entries.sig: (radius?: number, center?: PointLike, normal?: PointLike): Curve

entries.name: Compound
entries.doc:
Build a CompoundCurve from an ordered array of connecting Curves.
Rebuilds a joined polyline through the concatenated control points.

entries.name: Ellipse
entries.sig: (radiusX?: number, radiusY?: number, center?: PointLike, rotation?: number, normal?: PointLike): Curve
entries.doc:
Build a full ellipse (closed) with semi-axes `radiusX` (major direction)
and `radiusY` (minor direction), its major axis rotated `rotation` degrees
in-plane, centred at `center`, in the plane whose normal is `normal`.
Backed by exact rational conic spans (not a sampled polyline).

entries.name: EllipticalArc
entries.sig: (radiusX?: number, radiusY?: number, startAngle?: number, endAngle?: number, center?: PointLike, rotation?: number, normal?: PointLike): Curve
entries.doc:
Build an elliptical arc (a portion of an ellipse) from `startAngle` to
`endAngle` (degrees, in the pre-rotation ellipse parameter). A full 360°
sweep yields a closed ellipse. Semi-axes `radiusX`/`radiusY`, major axis
rotated `rotation` degrees in-plane, centred at `center`.

entries.name: fromCsgrs
entries.doc: Wrap a native hypercurve Curve3DJs as a meshup `Curve`.

entries.name: fromCurve3D
entries.doc: Alias of fromCsgrs: the internal representation is now `Curve3DJs`.

entries.name: fromSketchJs
entries.doc:
Convert a csgrs `SketchJs` (2-D geometry) into meshup `Curve`s.

Each ring from `SketchJs.rings()` becomes one polyline `Curve` on the XY
plane (z = 0). Polygon exteriors and holes come back as separate
`closed: true` rings; LineStrings/Lines as `closed: false`. Degenerate
rings are skipped.

This is the inverse of Sketch._toSketchJs and the bridge the
Importer uses for SVG / GeoJSON / DXF import.

NOTE: rings are returned as a flat collection — hole↔exterior nesting is
not reconstructed, and source styling (SVG colors etc.) is not carried by
`rings()` and is therefore dropped.

entries.name: Interpolated
entries.doc: Make a NURBS curve by interpolating through given points

entries.name: Polyline
entries.doc: Make a polyline curve with corners given by control points

entries.name: Rect
entries.sig: (width: number, height: number, center?: PointLike, plane?: BasePlane): Curve
entries.doc: Create a closed rectangle centered at a given position on an optional base plane.

params.name: width
params.doc: size along the local X axis of the plane

params.name: height
params.doc: size along the local Y axis of the plane

params.name: center
params.doc: centre of the rectangle (default: origin)

params.name: plane
params.doc: base plane the rectangle lies on (default: 'xy')

entries.name: RectBetween
entries.sig: (from: PointLike, to: PointLike, plane?: BasePlane): Curve
entries.doc:
Create a closed rectangle defined by two opposite corner points.
The rectangle lies on the given base plane; if omitted, the plane is inferred
from the axis with the smallest span between the two points.

params.name: from
params.doc: first corner

params.name: to
params.doc: opposite corner

params.name: plane
params.doc: optional base plane override

entries.name: mode
entries.doc: Kernel a shape belongs to. meshup shapes are always the mesh kernel.

entries.name: addAnnotations
entries.doc: Link annotation(s) to this Shape (host-app side of the two-sided annotation link)

entries.name: addHole
entries.doc: Add a hole defined by an array of PointLike vertices

entries.name: addToScene
alt: (): this
entries.doc:
Add this shape to the scene, under the active layer of the scene it is bound to.
Clears the sticky `tmp()` flag — `addToScene()` is the documented way back in.

`scene` may be given explicitly (the usual case for a host that owns a root and is
adding a freshly built, never-attached shape); otherwise the shape's own node/carried
root is used. Returns `this` even when no scene is reachable, so it stays chainable.

entries.name: align
entries.sig: (other: AlignTarget, pivot?: string | PointLike, alignment?: string | PointLike): this
entries.doc:
Translate this shape so that the `pivot` point on its own bbox coincides with
the `alignment` point on `other`'s bbox.

Both `pivot` and `alignment` accept:
- A keyword string combining any of: left, right, front, back, top, bottom
  (unspecified axes default to the centre of that axis)
- A PointLike [x%, y%, z%] where 0 = min-side and 1 = max-side

`other` may be a Shape, a Point, or a raw PointLike; a point is treated as a
zero-size bbox at that location (as if it were a Vertex).
examples:
box.align(shelf, 'bottom', 'top')  // sits box on top of shelf
box.align(other, 'center', 'center') // centres box on other
box.align(curve.middle(), 'lefttop') // align to a bare point

entries.name: alignTo
entries.sig: (other: AlignTarget, pivot?: string | PointLike, alignment?: string | PointLike): this
entries.doc: Alias for align()

entries.name: annotations
entries.doc: Annotations linked to this Shape

entries.name: area
entries.doc: Area using triangle-fan cross-product method (works for planar polygons in 3D)

entries.name: autoDim
entries.sig: (options?: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }, strategy?: string): any
entries.doc:
Automatic dimensioning of this shape (Annotator). `dim()` routes here by itself
for shapes a single bbox dimension cannot describe.

params.name: options
params.type: { offset?: number; offsetVec?: unknown; ortho?: boolean | "x" | "y" | "z"; roundDecimals?: number; showUnits?: boolean; units?: "mm" | "cm" | "dm" | "m" | "km" | "inch" | "feet" | "yd" | "mi" }

entries.name: autoRotate
entries.doc:
Rotate this Polygon to align as much as possible to the world axes.
Alias for rotateToOrtho()

entries.name: bbox
entries.doc: Axis-aligned bounding box of this polygon

entries.name: carbon
entries.doc: Embodied carbon (kgCO2e) of this shape. Defaults to cradle-to-gate A1-A3.

entries.name: center
entries.doc:
The area centroid of the polygon — what "centre" means for a face, and the same answer
the brep kernel gives for a Face. (This used to average the vertex ring, which counted a
repeated closing vertex twice and pulled the centre off for anything but a symmetric
ring: a 100×50 plane reported (−10, −5).) Falls back to the vertex mean for a degenerate
polygon with no area.

entries.name: color
entries.sig: (color: string | number, g?: number, b?: number): this

entries.name: copy
entries.doc:
Public copy. Clones via `_copy()`, then — unless this shape is `tmp()` — adds the
clone to the active layer. `copy()` means "give me a new shape", and new shapes render:
the clone is attached whenever a layer is reachable, which includes copying a DETACHED
but scene-derived shape (`curve.segments().first().copy()`) via the carried `_scene`.
The clone inherits the opaque `_modeler` and is flagged `_nameInherited` so the host
auto-namer can rename it after its variable.

Inside kernel operations use `_copy()` instead — it is the pure clone and never touches
the scene. Do NOT reach for `tmp()` there: `_suppressScene` is sticky and propagates to
every derived shape, so a tmp'd internal copy would suppress the real result too.

entries.name: cutoff
entries.sig: (at: Axis, coord?: number, smallest?: boolean): this
entries.doc:
Cut off this polygon orthogonally with an axis-aligned plane and keep one piece.

The cut is the line where the world plane `{ <at> = coord }` meets this polygon's plane
(its direction is polygonNormal × axisNormal). By default the largest piece (by area) is
kept; set `smallest=true` to keep the smallest. This is a planar (2D) cut — polygons are
flat, so it does not go through the solid boolean path used by Mesh.cutoff().

Mutates in place and returns `this`. Returns unchanged (with a warning) when the plane is
parallel to the polygon or does not actually split it.

params.name: at
params.doc: World axis of the cutting plane's normal ('x' | 'y' | 'z').

params.name: coord
params.doc: Position of the plane along `at` (default 0).

params.name: smallest
params.doc: Keep the smallest piece instead of the largest.

entries.name: cutoffBy
entries.doc:
Cut this polygon by another Polygon or Curve and keep one of the resulting pieces.
By default keeps the largest piece (by area); set `keepSmallest=true` to keep the
smallest. This is a planar (2D) cut delegated to split(), so the cutter may be open or
closed and is projected onto this polygon's plane (see split() for the full contract).

Mutates in place and returns `this`. If the cutter does not split the polygon into at
least two pieces, a warning is emitted and the polygon is left unchanged.

params.name: other
params.doc: Cutting Curve (open or closed) or Polygon.

params.name: keepSmallest
params.doc: Keep the smallest piece instead of the largest.

entries.name: difference
entries.doc:
Subtract a closed cutter — a closed Curve, a Polygon, or every shape in a
ShapeCollection — from this polygon (2D boolean difference). The cut runs on this
polygon's boundary curve (the same robust rust curve-boolean that split() uses) and
is applied in place; returns `this`.

 - A cutter that bites into the boundary leaves a notched polygon (one piece).
 - A band-like cutter that crosses the whole polygon splits it; the largest piece is
   kept (with a warning) — use split() when you want every piece.
 - A cutter that lies fully inside the polygon is not a boundary op and removes no
   area: use addHole() for an interior hole (a warning points this out).

The cutter must be planar; it is projected onto this polygon's plane first, so a cutter
drawn on a parallel/coincident plane still works. A missing/degenerate/failed cut leaves
the polygon unchanged (with a warning). Interior holes on this polygon are dropped.

params.doc: Closed Curve, Polygon, or ShapeCollection of them.

entries.name: distance
entries.doc: Minimum distance from this polygon surface to a point, vertex, curve, polygon, or mesh.

entries.name: edges
entries.doc:
Boundary edges of this Polygon as line Curves: the outer loop, then one loop per hole.
These are the polygon's real edges — NOT the edges of its triangulation. For those
(feature-angle filtered, useful for shading/silhouettes) use `toMesh().edges()`.

entries.name: extrude
entries.doc: Extrude this polygon into a closed solid Mesh.

params.name: length
params.doc: Distance to extrude.

params.name: direction
params.doc: Direction vector (default: polygon normal).

entries.name: first
entries.doc:
The first shape of a single Shape is the Shape itself.

Ops that MAY split — `cutoffBy()`, `difference()`, `intersections()` — answer with one
Shape or with a ShapeCollection depending on the geometry, and a script cannot know which
in advance. `first()` lets the same line read either: `post.cutoffBy(diagonal).first()`.
brep's Shape carries the same method for the same reason.

entries.name: flip
entries.doc: Flip winding order and vertex normals in place

entries.name: hasHoles
entries.doc: Whether this polygon has interior holes

entries.name: holeCount
entries.doc: Number of interior holes

entries.name: intersection
entries.doc:
Keep only the area this polygon shares with another closed shape (planar boolean AND).

Polygons are flat, so there is no solid boolean to fall back on: the operation runs on
the boundary curves, exactly like difference(). The other shape must be closed and
planar; it is projected onto this polygon's plane first, so a shape drawn on a
parallel/coincident plane still works.

NON-REPLACING: this Polygon is left exactly as it is; the shared area comes back as a NEW
Polygon that is added to the active layer, so it is visible without an explicit
addToScene(). Mark this Polygon tmp() to keep the result out of the scene. When the shapes
do not overlap, or the boolean fails, the result is an unchanged copy and a warning is
emitted. Interior holes on this polygon are dropped.

params.name: other
params.doc: Closed Curve, Polygon, or ShapeCollection of them (applied in sequence).

entries.name: is3D
entries.doc:
Whether this Shape has extent along all three axes — the complement of is2D(), which
Mesh and Curve each define from their bbox. Kept on the base class because callers
outside meshup (the host annotator deciding which way to offset a dimension line) ask
any Shape, and a missing method there is a crash, not a `false`.

entries.name: isCurve
entries.doc: True for curve-like shapes: mesh Curve (brep Edge/Wire once wired).

entries.name: isFlatOnXY
entries.doc:
True when this Polygon lies on a plane parallel to XY — a face SVG can draw as it is,
rather than a face SVG would have to project. What flatten() leaves behind.

is2D() cannot answer this: every Polygon is planar, so it is always true, including
for a wall standing up in Z which projects to a single line.

entries.name: isShapeClass
entries.doc: Implement this and ShapeCollection allows it

entries.name: isSolid
entries.doc: True for solid-like shapes: mesh Mesh (brep Shell/Solid once wired).

entries.name: label
entries.sig: (value: string, options?: { angle?: number; arrow?: boolean; circle?: boolean; class?: string; labelOnly?: boolean; length?: number; … }): any
entries.doc: Attach a free-text label at this shape's center (Annotator).

params.name: options
params.type: { angle?: number; arrow?: boolean; circle?: boolean; class?: string; labelOnly?: boolean; length?: number; … }

entries.name: layflat
entries.doc:
Rotate this polygon so it lies flat on the XY plane (its normal pointing +Z) and drop
it onto z = 0. Unlike Mesh.layflat(), which has to guess the thin axis from an oriented
bounding box, a Polygon has an exact plane normal to rotate. Mutates and returns `this`.

entries.name: length
entries.doc: Alias for perimeter

entries.name: loft
entries.sig: (others: Curve | Polygon | (Curve | Polygon)[], solid?: boolean): Mesh | Polygon
entries.doc:
Loft from this polygon's boundary to one or more other profiles, giving a solid Mesh.

This polygon's boundary is a closed curve, so lofting to another closed profile caps
both ends into a watertight solid (see Curve.loft()). Polygon profiles are used as their
closed boundary; open profiles are lofted as-is into a surface.

params.name: others
params.doc: A single Curve/Polygon or an array of them to loft through (in order).

params.name: solid
params.doc: Cap the ends into a watertight solid when all profiles are closed (default true).

entries.doc: Assign (setter, chainable) or read (getter → BoundMaterial) this shape's material.

entries.doc: Move this shape so its bbox centre lands on `target`

alt: (): string
entries.doc:
Get or set a name for this shape (stored in metadata).
- Called with a string: sets the name and returns this (chainable).
- Called with no arguments: returns the current name or undefined.

entries.name: nodeString
entries.doc:
Scene membership of this Shape, as shown by every toString(): the node holding it,
or that it is not in the scene at all.

entries.name: obbox
entries.doc:
Oriented bounding box of this polygon: the tightest (minimum-area) box around it.
A Polygon is planar by construction, so the exact route always applies — no need to
drop duplicate vertices first the way Curve does, since the hull ignores them.

entries.name: offset
entries.doc:
Offset this polygon's boundary by `distance` (positive = outward, negative = inward).

Polygons have no native offset, so we route through Curve: the boundary is
converted to a closed planar Curve, offset there, then converted back to a
Polygon. Returns null when the offset fails or degenerates.

params.name: distance
params.doc: Offset distance; positive grows the polygon, negative shrinks it.

params.name: cornerType
params.doc: How to treat convex corners (passed through to Curve.offset).

entries.doc: Make this shape clickable in the viewer and react to selection.

entries.name: perimeter
entries.doc: Total perimeter — sum of all edge lengths

entries.name: plane
entries.doc: Get the polygon's plane

entries.name: polygonMetadata
entries.doc: Get the WASM polygon metadata as a JSON string, or undefined if none

entries.name: removeFromScene
entries.doc: Remove this shape from the scene (detaches its SceneNode). Returns `this`.

entries.name: resetStyle
entries.doc:
Drop every style set on this Shape, back to the defaults.

A fresh Style rather than a cleared one, so the "explicitly set"
bookkeeping resets too: after this the Shape contributes nothing of its
own to the scene's style cascade, exactly as if it had never been styled.
That is the difference between this and setting the properties back to
their default values by hand, which would keep overriding a parent.

entries.name: revolve
entries.sig: (angle?: number, axisStart?: PointLike | Axis, axisEnd?: PointLike | Axis, segments?: number): Mesh
entries.doc:
Revolve this polygon around an axis into a Mesh — the lathe.

The boundary is a closed curve, so a full turn gives a watertight solid and a partial
one is shut with a flat cap at either end (see Curve.revolve()). Interior holes are
carried across and revolved into a cavity — unlike extrude(), which drops them.

params.name: angle
params.doc: Sweep in degrees, negative to sweep the other way. Default 360.

params.name: axisStart
params.doc: Axis base point — or the axis direction, when `axisEnd` is left out.

params.name: axisEnd
params.doc: A second point on the axis.

params.name: segments
params.doc: Facets around the sweep.

entries.sig: (angleDeg: number, axis?: PointLike | Axis, pivot?: PointLike): this

entries.name: rotateQuaternion
entries.sig: (wOrObj: number | { w: number; x: number; y: number; z: number }, x?: number, y?: number, z?: number): this

params.name: wOrObj
params.type: number | { w: number; x: number; y: number; z: number }

entries.name: rotateToAxesOBbox
entries.doc:
Rotate this Polygon so its oriented bounding box lines up with the world axes:
the OBB's thinnest axis onto +Z first, then its longest axis onto +X.
A Polygon is planar, so its thinnest axis is the plane normal: this lays it flat on
the XY plane (without moving it there — use layflat() for that).
Position of the center is kept.

entries.name: rotateToOrtho
entries.doc:
Rotate this Polygon to align it with the world axes as much as possible.

First `rotateToAxesOBbox()` lays the polygon flat on the XY plane, then it is turned
around Z so its dominant edge direction lands on the X or Y axis. The second step only
ever turns around Z (by at most a quarter turn), so it can never undo the first.

params.name: o
params.doc:
'vertical' (default) puts the dominant edge direction on the Y axis,
'horizontal' puts it on the X axis

entries.sig: (from: PointLike, to: PointLike, pivot?: PointLike): this
entries.doc: Rotate this Polygon so vector `from` points along `to`, around `pivot` (default: center)

entries.name: scale
entries.doc: Scale Polygon with a uniform factor or per-axis [sx, sy, sz] around an origin (default: center of this Polygon)

entries.name: select
entries.doc:
Select (sub)shapes with a selector string (see Selector.ts).
Delegates to the single-polygon Mesh so all Mesh selectors work here too.

entries.name: selected
entries.doc: True when this shape is currently selected (clicked) in the viewer.

entries.name: setId
entries.doc:
Overwrite this shape's id. Ids are minted per construction, so a shape rebuilt from
a saved document would otherwise come back with a fresh uuid and lose every reference
to it (scene links, host selection, undo entries). Deserialisers call this to restore
identity; nothing else should.

entries.name: setMetadata
entries.doc: Set JSON-serializable metadata

entries.name: sid
entries.doc: Serial id: the order this shape entered the scene, or 0 if it never did. See `_sid`.

entries.name: split
entries.doc:
Split this polygon into two (or more) polygons with a cutting Curve or Polygon.

The actual cutting is done by the robust Rust-layer curve boolean:
 - An OPEN cutter (a line/curve that crosses the polygon) is turned into two large
   half-plane regions, one on each side of the cut, and the polygon is intersected
   with each — yielding one clean piece per side. This avoids relying on a single
   boolean to "fall apart" into two, which the underlying curve boolean does not do
   reliably for axis-aligned cuts. The cut is extended past both ends so it only has
   to *pass through* the polygon, not reach its edges exactly.
 - A CLOSED cutter (closed Curve or Polygon) is subtracted directly; if it spans the
   polygon like a band, the result naturally falls into multiple pieces.

Guards & warnings:
 - The cutter must be planar. It is projected onto this polygon's plane, so a cutter
   drawn on a parallel/coincident plane still works (any plane, not just XY).
 - Self-intersecting cutters are rejected (see Curve.selfIntersecting()) to avoid
   degenerate, overcomplicated split shapes.
 - If the result does not actually split into ≥2 pieces (e.g. the cutter misses the
   polygon), a warning is emitted and `null` is returned.
entries.returnsDoc: ShapeCollection<Polygon> of the resulting pieces, or null if no split happened.

params.name: other
params.doc: Cutting Curve (open or closed) or Polygon.

params.name: gap
params.doc:
Optional seam width left between the pieces (default 0 = exact split,
pieces meet along the cut). A positive value removes a strip of this
width centred on the cut.

entries.name: strokeWidth
entries.doc:
Line width in SCREEN PIXELS — not model units.

It travels to the viewer as `BENTLEY_materials_line_style.width` and becomes a pixel
`linewidth` on the fat-line material, so a line keeps the same apparent weight however
far you zoom. `thickness(4)` is four pixels, not four millimetres.

entries.name: subdivideTriangles
entries.doc: Subdivide triangles by the given number of levels

entries.name: subtract
entries.doc:
Subtract one or more closed cutters (each a Curve, Polygon, or ShapeCollection) from
this polygon in place. Alias-style convenience over difference(); returns `this`.

entries.name: thickness
entries.doc: Alias for `strokeWidth()`. Reads more naturally for a curve. Screen pixels.

entries.name: tmp
entries.doc:
Mark this shape as temporary: detach it from the scene AND set a sticky
`_suppressScene` flag so that every subsequent scene op (copy/extrude/split/…) on it
is a no-op and every shape derived from it is `tmp()` too. Ideal for building helper
geometry inside advanced methods. `addToScene()` (host) clears the flag. Returns `this`.

entries.name: toCurve
entries.doc:
This polygon's outer boundary as a closed Curve. Interior holes are not included.
The Curve is a fresh, scene-less shape - the caller places it if it needs to be visible.

entries.name: toMesh
entries.doc: Polygon is basically Mesh with one polygon

entries.name: toSVG
entries.doc: Export this Polygon as a self-contained SVG string, drawn from above (see toSVGElem).

entries.name: toSVGElem
entries.sig: (cssClass?: string, styleOpts?: { nonScalingStroke?: boolean; omitDefaults?: boolean }): string
entries.doc:
Return just the SVG element for this Polygon — a `<polygon>`, or a `<path>` when it has
holes — without the outer `<svg>` wrapper. Used by Mesh, ShapeCollection and SceneNode
to compose a drawing.

The face is drawn as seen from above: x and y straight through with y negated (SVG's y
axis points down), z dropped. That is exact for a face lying on a plane parallel to XY
and a projection for anything else — see isFlatOnXY(), which is what the collection
exporter filters on so a standing wall is never silently flattened to a line.

Holes leave as extra subpaths of ONE `<path>` with `fill-rule="evenodd"`, not as
elements of their own: a separate element would be filled in as solid as its parent the
moment the face carries a fill, and the hole would disappear.

`styleOpts` is passed straight to Style.toSvgAttrs — see there for why
non-scaling-stroke is opt-in and what omitDefaults is for.

entries.sig: (px: PointLike, dy?: number, dz?: number): this

entries.name: triangulate
entries.doc: Triangulate this polygon into triangular polygons

entries.sig: (at: Axis, coord?: number, smallest?: boolean): this
alt: (other: Curve | Polygon, keepSmallest?: boolean): this
entries.doc: Trim this polygon with an axis-aligned plane — the same as cutoff().

entries.name: union
entries.doc:
Merge another closed shape into this polygon (planar boolean OR). Same boundary-curve
contract as intersection(): closed + planar operand, projected onto this polygon's plane,
mutates in place and returns `this`. Shapes that do not touch cannot merge into one
polygon — the largest region is kept and a warning is emitted.

params.name: other
params.doc: Closed Curve, Polygon, or ShapeCollection of them (applied in sequence).

entries.name: vertices
entries.doc: Vertices of this polygon as a ShapeCollection of Vertices (position + normal preserved)

entries.name: weight
entries.doc: Mass/weight in the active unit system. Shortcut for material().weight().

entries.name: wireframe
entries.doc:
Turn this Polygon into a plain wireframe: its boundary and hole edges as Curves, no
hidden-line removal. Same edges as edges(), but this REPLACES the Polygon in the scene.

entries.name: bboxOf
entries.doc:
Bbox of anything an alignment can target: a Shape, a ShapeCollection, or a bare point.
A Point / PointLike behaves like a Vertex: a zero-size bbox at that location.

entries.name: bboxPercToPoint
entries.doc: Resolve a [x%, y%, z%] percentage triple to a world-space Point within `bb`.

entries.name: bboxPointOf
entries.doc:
Resolve an alignment spec — a corner keyword ('lefttop') or a [x%, y%, z%] triple —
to a world-space Point on `bb`.

entries.doc: Wrap an existing PolygonJs instance

entries.name: planeBetween
entries.doc:
Create a planar rectangular Polygon spanning between two points.
Mirrors Mesh.planeBetween() but yields a single Polygon instead of a Mesh.

entries.name: annotations
entries.doc: Annotations linked to this collection (for the host annotator / DXF export).

entries.name: addAnnotations
entries.doc:
Link annotations (dimension lines, labels) to this collection. Mirrors
Shape.addAnnotations() and the brep ShapeCollection's, which is what the host
annotator calls when it links an auto-dimension to the collection it measured.

entries.name: addToScene
entries.doc:
Add every shape in this collection to the scene, clearing their sticky `tmp()` flag —
the collection twin of Shape.addToScene(). `name` names the COLLECTION, not each member
(naming every shape the same would make the scene unreadable). Returns `this`.

entries.name: align
entries.sig: (other: AlignTarget, pivot?: string | PointLike, alignment?: string | PointLike): this
entries.doc:
Move the whole collection so that the `pivot` point on its combined bbox lands on the
`alignment` point of `other`. Same contract as Shape.align(), but the collection is
moved as one unit — the shapes keep their positions relative to each other.
examples:
parts.align(base, 'bottom', 'top')      // sits the whole group on top of base
parts.align(other, 'center', 'center')  // centres the group on other

entries.name: alignTo
entries.sig: (other: AlignTarget, pivot?: string | PointLike, alignment?: string | PointLike): this
entries.doc: Alias for align()

entries.name: all
entries.doc: All shapes as a plain array (shallow copy).

entries.name: at
alt: (index: number, end: number): ShapeCollection<S>
entries.doc:
Access a shape by index, or a range of shapes when `end` is given.
- `at(i)`      → the shape at `i` (or undefined if out of range).
- `at(i, end)` → a ShapeCollection of shapes from `i` to `end` INCLUSIVE.
Negative indices count from the end (`at(-1)` = last), and a reversed range
(`at(5, 2)`) is normalised to `at(2, 5)`.

entries.name: autoDim
entries.doc: Automatic dimensioning of the shapes in this collection (Annotator).

entries.name: carbon
entries.doc: Total embodied carbon (kgCO2e) of the materialized shapes in this collection.

entries.name: closestPair
entries.sig: (other: ShapeCollection<Mesh>): { distance: number; mesh1: Mesh; mesh2: Mesh }

entries.name: colorGradient
entries.doc:
Give every Curve in this Collection the same gradient along its own length.

Each shape runs the full ramp individually — this does NOT spread one ramp across the
collection — which is how `.color()` and `.dashed()` already behave.

Shapes that cannot carry a gradient (Meshes, for now) are skipped, as with `.dashed()`.
See Curve.colorGradient for the accepted argument forms.

entries.doc: Merge connected curves in this collection into as few Curve/CompoundCurve objects as possible.

entries.name: connect
entries.doc: Connect curves in this collection into one, bridging small gaps where needed.

entries.doc:
Draw every Shape in this Collection as an unbroken line — the counterpart of
dashed. Sets the empty dash pattern EXPLICITLY on each shape, so it wins over
a dashed layer above them.

drop the doubles that creates — both across shapes (two identical walls flattened
onto the same rectangle) and within them (see Mesh.flatten() / Curve.flatten()).

shapes. Callback receives (groupName, collection, index).

entries.name: getAnnotations
entries.doc:
Every annotation linked to this collection or to a Shape in it. Mirrors the brep
ShapeCollection's getAnnotations() — what toSVG() draws.

entries.name: getGroup
entries.doc:
The shapes of a named group, or undefined when there is no such group.
Groups come from addGroup()/tagGroup() and from adding a NAMED sub-collection
(see add()). Also reachable as a shortcut property: `table.spine`.

entries.name: grid
entries.sig: (cx?: number, cy?: number, cz?: number, spacing?: PointLike): ShapeCollection<S>
entries.doc:
Copy this collection in a 3D grid, spaced uniformly or per axis.

Counts are floored and clamped to at least 1: `grid(4, 3, 0)` reads as "a flat 4x3
grid in XY", not "no copies at all" - a zero count on the unused axis used to return
an empty collection, so nothing showed up in the scene.

`spacing` is the distance between copy ORIGINS (unlike row(), where it is the gap
between bounding boxes). The shapes of this collection form the cell at [0,0,0]
themselves (like row()), so the scene never gets a duplicate set on top of them.

entries.name: groupNames

entries.name: hide
entries.doc: Hide Shapes in Collection

entries.name: intersecting
entries.doc:
The shapes in this collection that touch or intersect `other` — a filter, not a
geometry operation (see intersections() for the intersection geometry itself).
Shapes that only touch (a shared endpoint, an edge lying on `other`) count as
intersecting, which is what selections like "edges on this bbox side" rely on.

entries.doc:
Get only the first intersection (of possibly many) — a Curve or Mesh. Returns null
if none. Same non-replacing, added-to-the-active-layer contract as intersections().

entries.name: intersections

Intersect every shape with `other`, aggregating results.

NON-REPLACING: the collection's own shapes stay in the scene exactly as they are; the
results are NEW shapes added to the active layer, so they are visible without an
explicit addToScene().

entries.sig: (cam?: PointLike, method?: HlrStrategy, options?: ProjectionOptions): ShapeCollection<any>

entries.sig: (cam?: PointLike, method?: HlrStrategy, options?: ProjectionOptions): ShapeCollection<any>
